name: Golden Enoki
summary: Golden Enoki is the wild-type, gold-capped form of enoki. Same species as white enoki, grown with more light and air for shorter stems and amber caps.
notes: Sold as golden enoki or golden needle mushroom. Same species as the Enoki profile.
chamber_notes: A Shrooly cannot reach true cold-room enoki temperatures. This uses the coolest firmware target and more light than white enoki so caps color up.

source_notes.title: Stamets
source_notes.detail: Paul Stamets, Growing Gourmet and Medicinal Mushrooms (commonly cited chamber ranges). F. velutipes fruits cold, about 10 to 16 °C, at 90 to 95% RH.

source_notes.title: Vendor cards
source_notes.detail: Published grow-card ranges from culinary spawn suppliers (FreshCap, North Spore, Out-Grow and similar). Golden enoki kits list cool fruiting with indirect light for color.

stages.name: Pinning
stages.notes: Keep still and wet to pile up pins.

stages.name: Fruiting
stages.notes: Light brings out the gold cap color.

light_recipe.why: Golden enoki is the wild-type form of F. velutipes. No variety-specific lux was found, so this is the labeled general default. Light is what colors the caps.
light_recipe.wavelength_note: WS2812 blue is roughly 465 to 475 nm. The RGB mix is an approximation of cited wavelengths, not a measured spectrum.

sources.title: General default
sources.detail: No variety-specific photoperiod or lux was found for this species. Colonization is dark (Sakamoto 2018; Penn State oyster spawn run). Fruiting uses 12 h as a labeled default, not a page-cited Stamets value, and 20% white, which is 92 lux on this chamber, inside the Penn State oyster 50 to 300 lux band. Blue 80% approximates the 440 to 470 nm finding. This is a labeled default, not a measured value for this variety.

sources.title: Sakamoto 2004 enoki
sources.detail: Yuichi Sakamoto, Influence of light on the morphological changes that take place during the development of the Flammulina velutipes fruit body, Mycoscience 45 (2004). A temperature drop induces fruiting in the dark. Dark fruits are long, pale, and pinhead. Light then forms a cap.

sources.title: Stamets
sources.detail: Paul Stamets, Growing Gourmet and Medicinal Mushrooms, Ten Speed Press. Used here as a general cultivation reference. This recipe does not take a photoperiod or lux number from a cited page in that book.
